announcements.title: The app is now live on the App Store
announcements.body:
After three weeks of wrangling with Apple, That Real Blind Tech Show is officially on the App Store. If you are reading this, you already have it. So do the next best thing and tell a blind friend, a low vision friend, or that one sighted person who keeps asking you what a screen reader is.

Ratings and reviews genuinely move the needle on whether anyone else finds this thing. If the app is working for you, a quick review on the App Store would be appreciated more than you know.

And if you are new here, head over to the Articles tab. There is a guide waiting that explains what you have gotten yourself into.

announcements.title: Welcome to That Real Blind Tech Show — The App!
announcements.body: You can now listen to all of your favorite episodes, newly released episodes, check out articles about us, written by us and about us, contact anyone from the show directly, and keep up with all of the team's latest projects. Make sure to enable push notifications to get notified of new episodes and new content!

articles.title: New Here? Start With This
articles.author: Brian Fischler
articles.body:
Welcome. If you just downloaded this app and have never heard the show, here is everything you need before you press play.

WHAT THIS IS

A podcast about the good and the bad of assistive technology for blind and low vision people. Over 200 episodes. VoiceOver, JAWS, Narrator, VoiceView, audio description, smart glasses, A.I., and basically anything that talks to you.

It is not NPR. It is an entertainment technology show, which means the tech gets covered properly and the conversation goes wherever it goes.

WHO YOU WILL HEAR

Brian Fischler, host, producer and editor. Ed Plumacher. Allison Meloy. Jeanine Stanley. David Goldstein. All of them are reachable from the Contact tab in this app, which you may come to regret.

THE RUNNING GAGS, EXPLAINED

First, a point of law. If you are blind, you are federally required to have a podcast. Look it up.

Fahrvergnugen. How does a blind tech show know it has arrived? When it needs an edit to avoid an adult rating so the kids can listen in. It is in the name — what you hear is what you get — except when somebody drops an F bomb. Rather than bleep it, Brian started editing in the greatest word in the English language: Fahrvergnugen. For anyone under forty, it comes from a cheesy 1980s Volkswagen commercial. We were never sure whether it was a car or a state of mind. You know you have arrived when someone recognizes you at a blind tech conference and opens with how the Fahrvergnugen are you.

The interns. Brian fires all the interns every Christmas. Full disclosure: the interns exist only in Brian's mind, along with a good deal else, including all the voices in there.

A standing disclaimer. Just because you heard it on That Real Blind Tech Show does not make it true. We cannot be held responsible for getting every detail right. They do not pay us enough.

THE SEGMENTS

Blind Feud. Brian leaves certain topics off the outline circulated before recording, so he can put Ed, Allison, Jeanine and David on the spot. He asks a question with only one or two correct answers. Nobody has yet found the number one answer on the board, though a co-host once landed the number two answer, at a point when there was only one answer on the board to begin with. Losers must kiss Richard Dawson on the lips.

What's Pissing Off Brian Now. As a blind guy there is a great deal that annoys Brian, and rather than rant at his family about it he started a podcast where he could complain about accessibility and assistive technology instead. It has since expanded to cover everything in life that has annoyed him between episodes. His co-hosts are welcome to contribute, though in Brian's view they do not take nearly enough advantage of it.

Watcha Streaming, Watcha Reading. The closer, and around almost since the beginning. With Brian's love of movies, and audio description now available on very nearly everything, the gang finish each episode on what they have been watching and reading. In six years of the show Brian has completed two books. The over under on books read by Brian is therefore set at one per year, and he has hit the under more than once.

Clauding. The newest segment, born out of hearing about other blind technologists building their own apps with A.I. Billion dollar corporations in 2026 still find ways to overlook accessible design, and the excuses are genuinely baffling. So Allison, Jeanine and eventually Brian went down the rabbit hole to see what they could build themselves. VibeCoding is a misleading name, since you are not coding at all, you are building through natural language. If you can follow step by step directions, have some patience and some imagination, and are sick of waiting for companies to fix their broken products, you can build it yourself. The app you are holding is one of the results.

THE MUSIC

Brian wrote the show's theme and the jingles for its segments. Lyrics by Brian, built with A.I., assembled and mixed by hand. Critics say the theme is the greatest rock song released in the past twenty years. The critics in question are the interns, who no longer work here.

THE EDITING

Every episode is edited by Brian, and that is not a formality.

A show that sounds like five people in a room talking in real time is usually nothing of the sort. This one is recorded multitrack, and what you hear has been assembled — clips, drop ins, sound effects, timing tightened — so cleanly that nobody hears the joins. Every burp, cough, snort and sneeze that is not funny comes out. Deep breaths do not make the show.

An hour long episode takes two to three hours to edit, depending on how rough the source audio is. Brian works in Reaper on the Mac with OSARA and SWS, the extensions that make a professional editing suite genuinely usable by a blind engineer.

Blind listeners are sound quality snobs, Brian very much included. Garbage in, garbage out. He learned during the pandemic, when New York City was locked down tighter than Alcatraz and he spent it eating industrial quantities of Doritos and hiring a teacher to show him how to edit. Time well spent.

HOW IT STARTED

Brian's first podcast was iAccessVO, about iOS accessibility. He then partnered with Blind Abilities to launch That Blind Tech Show. Both are now finished. That Real Blind Tech Show came next, and this one Brian owns outright. Over two hundred episodes so far, and it has become one of the more trusted voices in the assistive technology community, in between the nonsense.

WHERE TO START

Anywhere. Open the Episodes tab and pick something that sounds interesting. The show does not require homework.

For guests, feedback or sponsorship: thatrealblindtechshow@gmail.com. Everything else goes to Brian@LaughForSight.com.

articles.title: To A.I. or Not To A.I.
articles.author: Brian Fischler
articles.body:
As someone who was initially against A.I. — boy, and girl, have I come around.

Let me clarify that statement. I was always pro-A.I. for the tasks that actually help the blind: identifying products, scanning labels, finding a door — that whole "last ten feet" problem where GPS proudly gets you to the building and then abandons you on the sidewalk like a bad date. What I was against was A.I. for writing. As a professional comedian of 20 years, with an even longer background in writing, my thinking was pretty simple: who the hell needs A.I. to write for them?

I still rarely let A.I. write for me. But I did use it to knock out a quick LinkedIn post for Laugh For Sight, and I'll admit it — I was pleased with the results. Don't tell anyone.

Here's what truly floored me. In under a year, we've gone from people using A.I. to write their emails to people using A.I. to build entire apps — like the That Real Blind Tech Show app you're reading this in right now.

I knew exactly what I wanted in this app. With Claude, it took me less than an hour to build it. It then took Apple 18 hours to approve it for beta testing. So let the record show: Apple took at least 18 times longer to approve this app than I took to build the thing.

I can't wait to see where we go next. And yes — before you ask — I wrote this one myself.
